name: Book Like A Boss
tagline: Booking pages for services, events, products, and payments

pricing.basis: paid plan; billing basis requires review
pricing.native: Public paid plan exists; amount not safely recovered
pricing.notes: The official pricing URL is recorded, but a stable current amount was not safely recoverable in this pass. Do not publish a number until rechecked.

tiers.name: Espresso
tiers.limits: Unlimited free bookings/meetings, SMS reminders, group bookings, embeds and integrations

tiers.name: Mocha
tiers.limits: Espresso features plus custom domain and removal of Book Like A Boss branding/footer

tiers.name: Cappuccino
tiers.limits: Paid bookings, coupons, events/classes, recurring appointments and memberships
tiers.notes: Freelancer plan; does not include the full white-label/custom-domain bundle.

tiers.name: Latte
tiers.limits: All sales features plus custom domain, removed branding and advanced customization

tiers.name: Teams
tiers.limits: Minimum 3 users; team scheduling/admin and 100 SMS credits per seat
tiers.notes: Current official team page exposes $8.50/user/month billed yearly; exact month-to-month price was not exposed.

pricing.billingTerms: monthly + annual for freelancer plans; Teams annual price exposed; 14-day trial, no card; subscriptions auto-renew
pricing.hiddenCosts: Teams has a 3-seat minimum. Teams Pro costs an additional $5/seat/month and doubles SMS credits from 100 to 200 per seat while adding white-label/admin customization. Book Like A Boss takes 0% of sales, but Stripe/PayPal processing fees still apply.

verdictSummary: The visible booking storefront loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Book Like A Boss earns its keep through OAuth, calendar reliability, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a personal booking storefront tool that reads one calendar, publishes availability, reserves a slot, and writes the event back.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
whatYouLose: reliable reminders and timezone edge cases
whyPeopleStillPay: Book Like A Boss: People pay because a booking tool must never double-book them, leak private events, or send the wrong time to a client.
ongoingBurden: Maintain OAuth, timezone data, webhooks, idempotency, reminders, calendar-provider quirks, and uptime.

priorArt.name: Cal.com
priorArt.desc: Mature open-source scheduling platform and OAuth reference.

alternatives.name: Appointy Free
alternatives.desc: One staffer gets reminders, classes and Square checkout for 100 bookings a month; growth wakes the paywall.

facts.dataFormat: Booking, customer, service and staff records live in Appointy's cloud, with connected calendar and payment data also handled by their respective providers
facts.gapVsPaid: The free plan is capped at 100 appointments and five services and is less flexible for mixed service, product, package and landing-page sales.

alternatives.name: Setmore Free
alternatives.desc: Four staff, payments, classes and 200 monthly bookings; SMS, recurring appointments and two-way sync cost extra.

facts.dataFormat: Booking, customer and staff records live in Setmore's cloud, with calendar and payment records also passing through connected providers
facts.gapVsPaid: It stops at 200 appointments and is less flexible as a storefront for products, packages and richly customized booking pages.

alternatives.name: Square Appointments Free
alternatives.desc: A serious free solo booking stack where Square operates; processing fees remain and the feature mix varies by country.

facts.install: Create or use a Square seller account and enable Appointments
facts.dataFormat: Appointment, customer, staff and transaction records live in Square's cloud
facts.gapVsPaid: It is tied to Square's supported regions and payment ecosystem and is less flexible for mixed product, event and service landing pages.
facts.setupBlocker: A Square seller account and identity verification, and the service must be available in the user's country

alternatives.name: TidyCal Free
alternatives.desc: Unlimited one-person booking types and paid bookings on one calendar; group meetings and fancy emails cost extra.

facts.dataFormat: Account, connected-calendar, appointment and payment-integration records live in TidyCal and AppSumo's cloud services
facts.gapVsPaid: The free plan connects one calendar and omits group bookings, custom intake questions, reminders, CSV export and API access.

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Book Like A Boss is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Book Like A Boss, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Next.js 15 + TypeScript + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a personal booking storefront tool that reads one calendar, publishes availability, reserves a slot, and writes the event back.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: reliable reminders and timezone edge cases; multi-calendar conflict handling; race-free booking under load.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
